title: Freight Now Adds Up to $40 a Barrel to Delivered Cost of Oil
excerpt: Tanker costs have risen sevenfold in a year as Hormuz war risk, ship-to-ship transfers and scarce vessels add as much as $40.50 per barrel on U.S.-to-Asia voyages, squeezing refiners and rerouting global crude flows.
body:
• Shipping about 2 million barrels of U.S. crude to Japan on a very large crude carrier now costs about $81 million — roughly $40.50 per barrel, versus about $9 million, or $4.50 per barrel, a year earlier, according to Reuters reporting cited by OilPrice.com.
  • Goldman Sachs estimates the global average crude freight rate has surged above $20 per barrel from $3 a year ago — a sevenfold rise — with Middle East routes above $35 per barrel.
  • Goldman breaks the $20 rise into a $7 Hormuz war-risk premium, $4 for ship-to-ship transfers, $4 for higher marine fuel, $3 for inefficient tanker allocation and diversions, and $2 for restrictions on Iran's tanker fleet.
  • For refiners, especially in Asia, the choice is to pass higher freight on to consumers or accept lower margins — a cost readers ultimately see embedded in fuel prices, even though no tanker charge appears on a receipt.

The benchmark price of oil is only part of what a refinery pays. Transportation — long the cheapest, least visible link in the chain — has become a cost that can add roughly $40 to a single barrel on some routes, reshaping global crude flows.

Reuters recently reported that shipping roughly 2 million barrels of crude from the United States to Japan aboard a very large crude carrier (VLCC) could cost about $81 million, OilPrice.com wrote. That works out to approximately $40.50 for every barrel on the ship, compared with roughly $9 million for a similar voyage a year earlier.

Sevenfold in a Year

Goldman Sachs estimates the global average crude freight rate has surged above $20 per barrel from $3 per barrel a year ago — about seven times higher — with rates on some Middle Eastern routes rising above $35 per barrel, according to the bank's report as carried by ANI reporting on the Goldman note. Brent crude crossed $110 per barrel this week and was trading around $111.51 at the time of that reporting.

The increase began in the VLCC segment and on Middle Eastern routes but has since spread to all major crude trading routes, with long-distance voyages particularly affected. Goldman found transportation costs for crude shipped from West Africa to East Asia had also risen sharply, underlining that the spillover now reaches routes with no direct link to the Strait of Hormuz.

Where the $20 Comes From

Goldman decomposed the year-on-year rise into five parts. The war-risk premium for crossing the Strait of Hormuz contributes about $7 per barrel. Ship-to-ship transfers outside the Persian Gulf add $4, higher maritime fuel prices add $4, inefficient tanker allocation and increased vessel diversions add $3, and restrictions on the Iranian tanker fleet add $2.

War risk and ship-to-ship transfers together account for more than half of the increase. About one-sixth of tankers near the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman are engaged in ship-to-ship operations at any given time, tying up vessels that would otherwise be available for long-haul voyages. OilPrice.com noted that about 80 VLCCs have been tied up in and around the Gulf transportation system, according to Vitol's head of Asia — a shortage that helps explain why rates on unrelated routes have climbed as well.

Some VLCCs have recently generated daily returns of more than $1 million, compared with around $55,000 per day during 2025, OilPrice.com reported.

Refiners Squeeze, Flows Shift

Benchmark crude prices do not include transportation, so the freight surge lands directly on refiners' economics. "High freight rates may reduce refiners' overall demand for crude and/or skew it towards more closely located crude suppliers," Goldman said. Refiners with greater dependence on imported crude from distant suppliers — notably in Asia — "would have to either pass higher freight costs on to final consumers or accept lower net refinery margins," the bank added.

The shift is already visible. Freight from the U.S. Gulf Coast to Asia recently reached roughly $80 million per cargo, making some U.S. crude uneconomic for Asian refiners, Reuters reported. Buyers have looked instead to Middle Eastern or Latin American suppliers, and Asian refiners have turned to smaller tankers, long-term charters and delivered crude purchases.

Producers serving distant buyers may have to discount more heavily to keep demand, Goldman said, while crude from suppliers closer to consumption centres — Brent in north-west Europe and Russia's ESPO among them — may gain from demand reallocation.

What to Watch

Goldman said the five freight drivers "will likely continue to support global freight rates as long as the conflict in the Middle East persists," and that elevated freight poses upside risk to its Brent forecast, even though its baseline sees Brent falling to $90 per barrel by year-end. Rates have already retreated somewhat from their peaks, but supertanker rates remain elevated.

For consumers, there is no separate tanker line on a gasoline receipt. The cost is embedded — in refinery margins, in regional crude discounts, and ultimately in the price of gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.
